extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientifically-minded investigators
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and rules for legitimate induction: what induction is, how it differs from superficially similar operations, limits of tests like inconceivability, and special points about mathematical reasoning. Aimed at guiding correct inference from observed instances to general propositions or to individual unobserved facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is the operation of discovering and proving general propositions; the process by which we infer that what we know to be true in particular case(s) will be true in all cases which resemble the former in certain assignable respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes both establishment of general propositions and indirectly ascertaining individual facts; generals are collections of particulars (definite in kind, indefinite in number). Whenever evidence justifies inference about one unknown case it justifies similar inference about a whole class of cases. Induction is the main question of logic because all non-intuitive knowledge comes from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of induction is the same for general and individual inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles and rules of inference are the same whether we infer general propositions or individual facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus a complete logic of the sciences would be a complete logic of practical business and common life: the senses/testimony decide individual facts; syllogism interprets whether facts fit general propositions; the same conditions determine the legitimacy of the inductions themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction must proceed from known to unknown (requires inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is an operation of inference; processes that involve no inference (where conclusion is no wider than premises) are not genuine induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes real induction from mere abridged notation/summing up of known instances (what some logicians call 'perfect induction', e.g., asserting of each enumerated planet what is observed of each). Genuine induction infers beyond the observed instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real generalisation from abridged registration of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition that merely re-states a finite list of observed individuals is not a true general proposition and not an induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'All known animals have a nervous system' is merely summing known species; 'All animals have a nervous system' is a real induction (if used to predict yet-undiscovered species). The difference is whether the conclusion contains more than the premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of instances depends on number and nature, not exhaustiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the number and nature of the observed instances that can make them sufficient to prove a general law, not the fact that every member of the class has been examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We need not examine every known individual to establish a genuine general law; representative, well-chosen instances may suffice. Conversely, asserting 'all known' requires exhaustive verification of known items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconceivability of the negation is not a reliable criterion of impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no ground for inferring that a fact is impossible merely from our inability to conceive its possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test of inconceivableness (Spencer's Universal Postulate) fails in many historical cases (e.g., sunrise/sunset as sun's motion, antipodes, gravitation without medium). Inability to conceive a negation may reflect habit or limited imagination, not objective impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the inconceivability test is limited to simple propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The test that 'an abortive effort to conceive the negation shows the cognition is one we are compelled to accept' applies only to propositions assented to on simple inspection without intervening media of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex propositions (those reducible to many simple propositions) cannot legitimately be tested by immediate inconceivability. Mathematical truths requiring mediate proof (e.g., Pythagorean theorem) are such examples where direct inconceivability is not applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer appeal to experience over the inconceivability test
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, test a proposition by direct appeal to experience rather than by relying on whether its negation seems conceivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience (knowing one has seen the fact repeatedly and others with opportunity concur) bears on the sufficiency of evidence; inconceivability only indicates familiarity and may disguise insufficiency. Spencer's objection about the impracticability of recalling all instances is rebutted: it is enough that the fact has been repeatedly experienced and universally reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherited mental tendencies may make beliefs seem a priori but can be false
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental tendencies originally derived from experience may become ingrained and transmitted, making certain convictions appear innate or a priori, though they may be untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a conviction is 'innate' via inheritance of modes of thinking, it need not be true since the original tendency may have arisen from causes other than truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Contradiction grounded in experience (not merely verbal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assertion that a proposition cannot be both true and false is not mere verbal logic but a generalization from experience: belief and disbelief are distinct, mutually exclusive mental states, and positive/negative phenomena are typically contrasted externally as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus the Principium Contradictionis should be enunciated simply: the same proposition cannot at the same time be false and true; its foundation is observational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Excluded Middle requires qualification (the 'unmeaning' possibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle that every proposition must be either true or false holds only when the predicate is intelligibly attributable to the subject; otherwise a third possibility — the Unmeaning — exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Abracadabra is a second intention' is neither true nor false. Extensions of the principle to noumena (things-in-themselves) are unwarranted because predicates may be inapplicable or unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical generalisations are often not empirical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Many mathematical arguments that produce general propositions are not inductions in the empirical sense but are either summations of demonstrative proofs for each case or induction by parity of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proving a property for circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola and then asserting it for all conic sections is a summing up, not an empirical induction. Diagrams and demonstrative a priori reasons show the theorem for any instance; the generality follows from the demonstrative principle rather than observation of instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical extrapolation of series depends on a priori justification
rubrics_metrics.description: When mathematicians infer the law of a series and fill further terms, they rely on a priori considerations that the mode of formation will continue, not on mere empirical counting of many terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrapolation in series is justified when it is apparent from a priori reasoning that subsequent terms must be formed in the same manner as those already calculated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of which inductions to apply is a matter of sagacity and subject-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical inquiry (e.g., advocate before a jury), the chief difficulty lies in selecting appropriate inductions to apply; this selection depends on sagacity and knowledge, not on the formal rules of induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science can then tell whether the chosen inductions, when constructed into an argument, legitimately apply; but invention and selection of useful inductions cannot be fully reduced to rule.
